title: Study in pairs
hookLine: Jewish learning is often done in pairs, arguing over a text

cards: Two men in the Talmud studied together: Rabbi Yochanan, a great teacher, and Resh Lakish, who, the story says, had once been a bandit before he turned to learning.
Then Resh Lakish died, and Rabbi Yochanan was deeply pained. The rabbis tried to help. They sent him a sharp scholar to sit in the empty seat.
Every time Rabbi Yochanan said something, the new partner answered: there's a teaching that supports you. Every single time. It should have been a comfort.

teach.b: Here's what Rabbi Yochanan said, in the Talmud's telling. When I said something, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections, and I would give twenty-four answers, and so the matter became clear.
You tell me there's a teaching that supports me. Don't I already know I'm right?

That's chavruta. The word is Aramaic, close to chaver, a friend or companion, and it means study in a pair. In a traditional study hall, pairs sit across a table, one text open between them, reading aloud and arguing.
Not fighting: arguing toward the text. What does this line mean, why this word, what about the case it doesn't mention? The noise of a room full of pairs is part of the picture.

The Talmud reaches for a verse from Proverbs, in the King James: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The rabbis read it of two students who sharpen each other in learning.
And the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers gives advice in two short pieces: make yourself a teacher, and get yourself a companion. A partner who only nods leaves you where you started.
A partner who pushes back makes you say why.
This week turned from walking as prayer to Jewish ways: your own words, alone in a field; kavanah; Musar; the Omer; a hundred blessings.
Today, the one practice that needs a second person across the table.

how: In yeshivas and study halls, and in adult-learning programs, Jews study Talmud and other texts in pairs called chavrutas, reading aloud and questioning each other line by line.

o: a circle of students silently copying a scroll
a private teacher who answers all your questions
two people studying one text, out loud, together

p: there's a teaching that supports you
so a man sharpeneth his friend

s: in chavruta, the goal is to agree as fast as possible
a partner who only nods leaves you where you started. pushback makes you say why.
Rabbi Yochanan missed the objections of Resh Lakish
twenty-four objections, twenty-four answers, and so the matter became clear.
the Ethics of the Fathers pairs a teacher with a companion
make yourself a teacher, and get yourself a companion.

games.q: you're Rabbi Yochanan. your new study partner backs up every word you say with a supporting teaching. how do you respond?
o: thank him: it's good to be agreed with.
tell him you miss the objections that made things clear.
games.why: in the Talmud's telling, he says Resh Lakish raised twenty-four objections, and the answers made the matter clear. agreement taught him nothing.

practice: Take the line iron sharpeneth iron, say it once slowly, and ask what it means; then take the other side: when does a friend dull you instead of sharpening you? Let the two voices take turns and answer back, without hurrying.
If you pray, you can bring the question before God; if you don't, just let the argument breathe.

wordCard.voice: Chavruta. Study in a pair: two people, one text, and plenty of questions across the table. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: companionship, a study partnership; close to Hebrew chaver, friend.

carryVoice: Your line: two heads. The point of a partner isn't agreement. A week of Jewish ways, done.
